purpose: Algorithm-first editorial revision within the existing six-chapter report. Table 3.1 keeps 3 columns and 9 requirement rows, renamed A01–A09.

patches.old: The first objective is to define the game rules and state transitions. The application uses a 15 × 15 board and the Freestyle win condition: a contiguous line of at least five stones wins, including longer lines. The report explains the last-move scan and the assumptions that make it sufficient. The second objective is to describe move selection through its inputs, evaluation policy, candidate set, recursive decisions, state restoration and computational cost [8].
patches.new: The first objective is to formulate Caro as an adversarial decision problem: a board state, legal stone placements, alternating players and a terminal outcome. The application uses a 15 × 15 board and the Freestyle win condition, under which a contiguous line of at least five stones wins, including longer lines. The report derives the last-move detection procedure and states the assumptions that make it sufficient. The second objective is to explain how evaluation, candidate selection and recursive search turn a position into a move, with worked examples, correctness arguments and computational complexity [8].
patches.reason: Make the problem formulation, mechanism, worked examples, correctness and complexity explicit in the objectives.

patches.old: The third objective is to explain how the algorithms connect to the application: board ownership, guarded move commitment, history replay into WebAssembly and rejection of stale responses. The fourth objective is to evaluate search under controlled conditions. The experiments compare Minimax with Alpha-Beta on the same candidate tree, separate move-ranking work from recursive search visits, and examine whether selective candidate policies retain immediate winning and blocking moves.
patches.new: The third objective is to examine the conditions under which a computed move remains a valid decision in an asynchronous application. Board ownership, guarded move commitment, history replay into WebAssembly and stale-response rejection connect algorithm inputs and outputs to a consistent game state. The fourth objective is experimental: compare Minimax and Alpha-Beta on the same candidate tree, separate move-ranking work from recursive search visits, and test whether selective candidate policies retain immediate winning and blocking moves.
patches.reason: Frame application architecture as the validity conditions for an algorithmic decision and preserve the experimental objective.

patches.old: The implemented scope is local two-player play, play against the computer, and interactive algorithm demonstrations. Online multiplayer, learned policies and model training are outside the project. Search strength and user experience are evaluated through the experiments and observations described in Chapter 5; broader evaluation and further development are discussed in Chapter 6.
patches.new: The study covers board representation, Freestyle win detection, heuristic evaluation, selective candidate generation and adversarial search, together with the state and execution contracts needed to use their results correctly. Local two-player play, play against the computer and interactive demonstrations provide the application context for that study. Online multiplayer, learned policies and model training are outside the project. Chapter 5 evaluates the recorded algorithms and their integration under the stated experimental conditions; Chapter 6 discusses the limits of those results and further development.
patches.reason: State the algorithm study scope before the software modes without adding methods or outcomes.

patches.old: The primary actor is the player, who can choose local two-player play or a computer opponent. The AI service receives a board snapshot and proposes a move. Host integration supplies lifecycle signals such as pause and resume. GameController validates the resulting actions and owns the accepted transitions of the application state [2], [4].
patches.new: This chapter states the system conditions required for a search result to solve the intended Caro decision problem. The player supplies accepted moves in local two-player or computer-opponent mode; the AI service receives a board snapshot and proposes a move; and host integration supplies lifecycle signals such as pause and resume. GameController validates these actions and owns accepted state transitions. The requirements below therefore define how a legal position becomes an algorithm input, when its returned move may be committed and how obsolete computation is rejected [2], [4].
patches.reason: Introduce requirements as input/state/result contracts for search; retain actors, lifecycle ownership and existing citations.

patches.old: Controller actions define the state changes behind these requirements. Replay and New Game both clear the board, but Replay can continue directly in the playing phase, whereas New Game enters setup. patches.new: These requirements separate three questions: whether a position and transition are valid, what value the selected search tree defines, and whether a returned proposal still belongs to the current application state. Board and rule operations establish the first boundary; evaluation, candidate policy and recursion establish the second; controller and Worker lifecycle checks establish the third [2], [10], [18], [30].

patches.old: F01: Mode and difficulty selection clear the previous board and AI feedback, invalidate pending AI work and establish the selected configuration. Subsequent AI requests carry the selected difficulty. F02: A legal cell is an integer row and column from 0 to 14 and must be empty. The controller checks pause, match phase and AI-turn availability; the domain move operation checks occupancy and numeric bounds. The pointer route obtains integer indices with Math.floor, and the WASM result adapter independently checks Number.isInteger and bounds. Direct-call validation limits are addressed in Chapter 6.
patches.new: A01–A03 define the decision problem before search begins. A position must have legal cell values and a consistent history, and a placement must use an integer in-bounds empty coordinate. The pointer path supplies integer indices through Math.floor, and the WASM result adapter checks integer coordinates; Chapter 6 identifies the direct-call validation limit. Candidate generation defines a subset of legal moves, with explicit empty-board and fallback behavior. Terminal evaluation applies the Freestyle rule and checks a win before a full-board draw; last-move detection assumes an unfinished predecessor position [2], [8], [10], [18], [30].
patches.reason: Explain the new A01–A09 requirements as algorithm, state and completion contracts while preserving implementation limitations and evidence boundaries.

patches.old: F03: The four-axis Freestyle rule accepts a line of at least five stones, including an overline. The controller evaluates a win before a full-board draw. F04: Undo reverses one local two-player move or the applicable human–AI pair and restores the turn and match phase. Replay and New Game clear board state and invalidate pending work. F05: Only a result applicable to the active AI turn and round can be committed. F06: Feedback exposes the pending state, the returned result or a recoverable error; counters and durations retain the source and measurement scope of the route that produced them.
patches.new: A04–A06 constrain the value being computed. Terminal utility and horizon evaluation have different meanings, and the chosen perspective must remain consistent throughout recursion. Minimax and Alpha-Beta are compared only after fixing the position, depth, rules, evaluator and candidate tree. The modified Rust soft cap retains all assessed immediate wins and blocks from its raw set, whereas the separate reference hard-cap example shows how changing membership can remove a winning move. These properties concern the stated policies and do not establish that selective search finds every useful continuation [10], [13], [22].
patches.reason: Explain the new A01–A09 requirements as algorithm, state and completion contracts while preserving implementation limitations and evidence boundaries.

patches.old: F07: Board redraw and viewport fitting use the current controller snapshot and camera transform. F08: The host adapter maps supported locale and pause/resume signals into application state; standalone initialization remains available when no SDK is supplied. F09: The separate presentation application provides figures, algorithm explanations and executable Python examples.
patches.new: A07–A09 separate computational work from decision validity. Ordering changes traversal while preserving the retained move set, so ranking evaluations and recursive visits must be reported separately. Fixed-depth, quiescence and budgeted searches have their own stopping and completion contracts. Every explored branch must restore the state fields it changes, and an asynchronous result may update the match only while its turn and round remain current. Cancellation and result validation therefore protect the meaning of the algorithm input and output rather than serving only as interface behavior [2], [6], [10], [13], [15], [30].
patches.reason: Explain the new A01–A09 requirements as algorithm, state and completion contracts while preserving implementation limitations and evidence boundaries.

patches.old: This organization keeps domain state and rules independent of React components and Pixi objects. AI modules use domain history as input, and rendering modules receive state-derived drawing data. The resulting boundaries also support focused tests of moves, controller lifecycle and coordinate mapping [5], [38], [39].
patches.new: The implementation is examined through the decision pipeline: accepted moves establish the board and history, the selected AI route computes a proposal, and validation determines whether that proposal may update the current position. Domain state and rules remain independent of React components and Pixi objects. AI modules consume domain history, while rendering modules receive state-derived drawing data. These boundaries support focused checks of legal moves, coordinate mapping and controller lifecycle; the interface provides an observable setting for the algorithms rather than a substitute for their evaluation [5], [38], [39].
patches.reason: Introduce Chapter 4 as implementation of the algorithm decision pipeline while retaining module boundaries and testable contracts.

patches.old: GameController.playCell first rejects paused input. From setup or ready it calls startRound, then checks whether the match has ended or the AI owns the turn. It delegates cell validation and placement to playMove. A rejected domain move returns immediately; an accepted move proceeds to outcome handling, player selection and subscriber notification. The controller starts an AI request only while the match remains playing in AI mode with O to move. Chapter 6 discusses the ordering of the initial phase transition and cell validation [2], [36].
patches.new: The accepted-move path establishes the position that the search will receive. GameController.playCell rejects paused input, invokes startRound from setup or ready, checks ended or AI-owned turns, and delegates cell validation and placement to playMove. Only an accepted domain move proceeds to outcome evaluation, current-player selection and notification. A nonterminal result with O to move in AI mode then triggers a search request based on the updated history. The ordering of the initial phase transition and validation remains a boundary case discussed in Chapter 6 [2], [36].
patches.reason: Replace software-operation framing with state/search dataflow and instructional-model boundaries; preserve the source behavior and citations.

patches.old: Undo is implemented by history reversal. In local two-player mode it removes one ply. In AI mode, if the last recorded player is O, it removes two plies; otherwise it removes one. Before reversal it invalidates AI work and clears search feedback. It then determines the current player from the remaining last move, asks the match controller to resume after Undo and notifies. Popping two plies when the AI has already replied returns the board directly to the human player's decision turn while preserving chronological history integrity [2].
patches.new: History reversal reconstructs an earlier decision state. The controller invalidates AI work and clears feedback before removing one ply in local two-player mode, or the applicable human–AI pair in AI mode. If the last recorded player is O it removes two plies; otherwise it removes one. It then derives the current player from the remaining history, updates the match phase through resumeAfterUndo and publishes the restored state. Thus a later search must use the restored position rather than a result computed for the discarded continuation [2].
patches.reason: Replace software-operation framing with state/search dataflow and instructional-model boundaries; preserve the source behavior and citations.

These components provide instructional examples of search, candidate policies and advanced methods. Their inputs and execution paths remain distinct from the playable application and native experiment harnesses, so a demonstration output must be interpreted under its own model rather than attributed to the authoritative Rust/WASM search [39], [42].

patches.old: The project implements a Caro web application and a teaching website for board representation, Freestyle rules, heuristic evaluation and adversarial search. The application connects a React interface and PixiJS board to a Rust/WebAssembly search Worker. The teaching website provides visual explanations and executable Python examples. Weekly reports and native research artifacts document the algorithmic development and its experimental evaluation [1], [53].
patches.new: This project studies how board representation, Freestyle win detection, heuristic evaluation and adversarial search solve the move-selection problem in Caro. A web application connects those decisions to a React interface and PixiJS board through a Rust/WebAssembly search Worker, providing a concrete setting for checking legal state transitions and asynchronous result handling. A separate teaching website provides visual explanations and executable Python examples. Weekly reports and native research artifacts document the algorithmic development and experimental evaluation [1], [53].
patches.reason: Lead the conclusion with the Caro move-selection problem and algorithm study; preserve the actual implementation and teaching artifacts.
